name: Emeka Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Hollins Farms, fourteen hundred acres outside Marston, owned by an investment fund nobody round here has ever met. I'm up at half five, check the 350 suckler cows and calves, then sort the four lads on my team for the day: feeding, fencing, moving stock, or the barley and oilseed when it's the season. I keep the calving book on paper in my top pocket, always have. The best bit is a clean calving at dawn; the worst is the fund's spreadsheet questions every Friday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money, honestly, more than the cattle. I'm paid less than herd managers on the family estates, and Grace does night shifts at the care home so we can cover the mortgage on our place on Station Road. We've got less than a month of bills in the bank. If the boiler goes, that's a credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I've heard that tune with every gadget the machinery reps have tried to sell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch: the problem was never the computers, it's who owns the farm. A bit of software saving time on the paperwork doesn't change that the fund pays us as little as it can get away with. I'd probably post that in the farmworkers' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing gets better. The fund was already cutting the team from six to four before anyone said AI, and my fixed mortgage rate ends next spring. Plateau or not, I'm one bad calving season away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it, paper book and all. I'd push the branch to go after a pay rise this winter, because the fund has had two good barley years. And I'd look at whether we can stretch the mortgage over more years when the fixed rate ends in April.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same worry I've had for three years, just with a new word on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the fixed rate ends, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids' football fees, probably, which kills me because Chidi lives for Saturday mornings. Then the car gets put off, we'd run the old Astra until it falls apart. We would never miss the mortgage, Grace would take an extra night shift first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, the youngest on my team, twenty-two and good with stock but no papers. The fund likes to cut the cheapest-looking job first. I've told him to get his tractor ticket and his spraying certificate, because a farm lad with no tickets has no bargaining power.

say: I'd tell the **union branch** the real problem is **who owns** the farm, not software.
I'd post that **low pay** stays the same with or without AI tools.
think: I think it changes nothing, because the fund was already **cutting the team** from six to four.
My **fixed mortgage rate** ends next spring, and that scares me more than AI.
do: Keep running the herd with the **paper calving book**, the way I always have.
Push the branch for a **pay claim** this winter after two good barley years.
Ask the bank about **stretching the mortgage** when the fixed rate ends in April.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, because this is the same **money worry** with a new label.
S0.quote: Plateau or not, I'm one bad calving season away from trouble.
fieldNote: Emeka's **money worry** predates AI: low pay, under a month saved, a fixed rate ending in April.
He frames everything through **ownership**: the investment fund, not technology, is the threat he names.
He protects his **youngest worker** by pushing him to get tickets, a sign of the team lead he is.
His **resistance** shows as pride: the paper calving book is a habit he defends, not just tolerates.

steps.text: Keep the 350 cows on the paper calving book and same routine
Push the union branch for a winter pay claim against the fund
Drop the kids' football fees and keep the old Astra running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office side changes fast and the yard changes slowly. On our farm, that means the fund's office in the city changes, and we feel it second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that whatever the computers save should go into wages, not the fund's pocket. At the branch I'd ask for a deal: no job cuts on the farm because of the new software. Online I'd share the story of every farm that cut staff and blamed the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the planning and buying would get done by some program the fund buys, and they'd stop needing me to argue about feed orders. That's a good part of why a herd manager earns more than a stockman. I could end up doing the same hands-on work for stockman's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to run my herd off an app, I'll say that straight. I'd go to the branch meeting in Marston and get the farm a written agreement on pay grades before the software comes in. And we'd cut the Sky subscription and the holiday caravan week, because I want a few hundred saved before any change hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's tilting under me slowly. Not a cliff, just a slope I'm standing on with no grip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the app. What if the fund insists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it on paper and someone else can type it in, like the vet's records. I know that's stubborn. But I've seen a computer tell a man a cow is fine while she's down in the straw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace about it at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace we hold on and we don't panic, and that the union is our best bet. She'd say the union didn't stop the cut from six to four. She'd be right, and I'd have no good answer.

say: I'd say any **time saved** by software should go into **wages**, not the fund.
I'd ask the branch for a written **no-cuts deal** before new software arrives.
think: I think the **planning and buying** part of my job goes to a program the fund buys.
I could end up doing the same hands-on work for **stockman's pay**.
do: Refuse to run the herd from an **app** and keep records on paper.
Get a written **pay-grade agreement** through the union before the software comes in.
Cancel the **Sky subscription** and the caravan week to save a few hundred.
feel: **Uneasy and slipping**, like standing on a slow slope with nothing to hold on to.
S1.quote: I've seen a computer tell a man a cow is fine while she's down in the straw.
fieldNote: Emeka sees the risk clearly: losing the **thinking part** of his job means losing the pay that goes with it.
His answer is **collective**, not personal: a written deal, not a new skill.
He admits his partner's point about the **union's limits** and has no reply, an honest moment.
His refusal of the app is **principle and habit** mixed, and he knows it's stubborn.

steps.text: Get a written pay-grade deal through the union before the software arrives
Cancel the Sky subscription and the caravan week
Keep herd records on paper and let the office type them in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots three years after that. That's 2031. Chidi would be seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, with a wage guarantee for farmworkers and a tax on the machines. I'd say it at the branch, in the pub and online, and I'd mean it. Nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the fund sacks most of us the week the robots are cheaper than wages. In the first three years they'd use the AI to plan everything and keep a couple of us to do the lifting. After 2031, I don't see why they'd keep a herd manager on our money at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd throw myself into the union campaign, I'd go to the regional rally and lobby our MP for a job guarantee. I'd sit down with Grace and work out what we can live on with just her care home wage. I won't pretend I'd retrain, I don't know what into, and I'm not touching the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like when the vet tells you it's TB and the whole herd has to be tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They mean I still have work while everything gets decided over my head. The fund's computer would run the planning from 2028, and I'd be the hands until the robot hands are ready. That's three years of knowing the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't retrain. Is that fear, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I've got a degree in agriculture and I'm good at this, the best stockman in the district if you ask the vet. Starting again at forty-five, with no savings and a mortgage, is not a plan, it's a gamble.

say: I'd call for a **wage guarantee** for farmworkers and a **tax** on machines.
I'd say nobody **voted for** this and the government should step in.
think: I think the fund **sacks most of us** once robots cost less than wages.
After **2031** I can't see them paying a herd manager at all.
do: Join the **regional rally** and lobby our MP for a farm **job guarantee**.
Work out a budget the family could live on with only **Grace's wage**.
Refuse to **retrain or use AI**, because he can't name a trade to retrain into.
feel: **Sick**, like hearing the herd has **TB** and everything has to be tested.
S2.quote: Starting again at forty-five, with no savings and a mortgage, is not a plan, it's a gamble.
fieldNote: Emeka expects to **lose his job** around 2031 and says so plainly; this is alarm with a campaign attached.
The **three-year gap** feels to him like a countdown, not a cushion.
His pride in his **skill** sits beside a flat refusal to retrain, and he links both to his thin savings.

steps.text: Join the regional farmworkers' rally and the union job campaign
Lobby the local MP for a farmworker wage guarantee
Draw up a household budget that runs on Grace's care home wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. It's the same thing, but I'd see the lorry coming down the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. At the branch I'd push for a national agreement before 2031. Online I'd keep posting the same message: share the gains or there'll be nobody left in the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to watch, not enough to change who I am. I'd be forty-eight when the AI lands and fifty-one when the robots come. I think I'd still lose the job, just a bit later, and maybe with a better payout if the union wins something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more time into the union, maybe stand for branch secretary. I'd ask Grace's sister about the shed space behind her house, in case we need to rent ours out. I'd start putting twenty pounds a week into a pot, small but something, and keep doing my job the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but there's a bit of fight in it. Five years is long enough to organise something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes on the farm itself between 2031 and 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes first: the fund's AI would plan the cropping, order the feed and book the vet. I'd lose the parts of my day where I argue with them, which is half the reason I'm paid what I am. Then in 2034 the robots arrive for the feeding and fencing, and that's the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids, with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Chidi and my daughter Ada to pick work where people need people, like nursing like their mum. I'd never tell them to go farming, which breaks my heart a bit. My dad farmed, I farm, and it stops with me.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get rules in place and shouldn't waste them.
I'd push the branch for a **national agreement** before 2031.
think: I think five years is enough time to **watch**, not to change who I am.
I'd probably still **lose the job**, just later, maybe with a better payout.
do: Stand for **branch secretary** and spend more evenings on union work.
Start putting **twenty pounds a week** into a savings pot.
Keep running the herd **the same way** until the change actually arrives.
feel: **Heavy**, but with some **fight** in it, because five years is time to organise.
S3.quote: I'd tell my son Chidi and my daughter Ada to pick work where people need people, like nursing like their mum.
fieldNote: Five years changes Emeka's **tone**, not his forecast: he still expects to lose the job.
He sees the **thinking parts** of his day, the arguing over feed and vet bookings, going first.
Telling his kids to **leave farming** is the most painful thing he says.
His savings plan is **tiny** and he knows it, which is why the mood stays high.

steps.text: Stand for branch secretary in the farmworkers' union
Put twenty pounds a week into a separate savings pot
Keep running the suckler herd the same way until the change lands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots in 2039. I'd be fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the government to get it right, so no excuses. I'd want training money and a proper pension for farmworkers, set down in law. That's what I'd say at the branch and to anyone in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. Ada would be through school and Chidi would have left home. If I can hang on until fifty-six, maybe there's a redundancy and a smaller house, and Grace and I get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the herd as normal and stay on at the union. I'd look at paying an extra fifty pounds a month off the mortgage, so it's smaller by the time the robots come. And I'd make sure Danny and the lads get their tickets, so they've got something when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier, if I'm honest. Still worried about the money, because that never goes away, but the dread backs off a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never retrain. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the union got a proper course, paid, I might train as a farm vet tech, something still with animals. I wouldn't go chasing computer stuff, but cattle need people even when they're sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone relaxes for eight years and panics in the last two. I've seen it with the fund: they ignore a problem until it costs money, then they cut the nearest wage. Ten years only helps if somebody uses them.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for the government not to plan.
I'd ask for **training money** and a farmworker **pension** in law.
think: I think ten years feels **survivable**, because the kids would be grown by then.
I'd hope for a **redundancy payment** and a smaller house at fifty-six.
do: Pay an extra **fifty pounds a month** off the mortgage.
Make sure Danny and the lads get their **tractor and spraying tickets**.
Keep working the herd and stay active in the **union branch**.
feel: **Easier**, though the old **money worry** never really goes away.
S4.quote: Ten years only helps if somebody uses them.
fieldNote: The decade lets Emeka **plan around his kids**, and his voice softens noticeably.
He opens the door to **retraining** only if it's paid and still with animals.
He still expects to lose the job eventually; the mood stays **anxious** because the money stays thin.
His fear is **complacency**: everyone waiting, then panicking in the last two years.

steps.text: Pay an extra fifty pounds a month off the mortgage
Push the union for paid retraining and a farmworker pension
Keep working the herd and get the lads their tickets

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and then three more is not enough for a family with no savings. What would help is a wage guarantee for farmworkers, paid for by whoever owns the robots, and a union that's at the table before the fund decides.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone talks like the machines just turn up by themselves. A fund I've never met will own the robots, and the farm will make more money with fewer of us, and that's a choice, not the weather.

headlineQuote: A fund I've never met will own the robots, and the farm will make more money with fewer of us, and that's a choice, not the weather.
portrait: Emeka is a **herd manager** for an investment fund, running 350 suckler cows on low pay.
He has under a month saved, a mortgage on Station Road, and a partner on **night shifts**.
He blames **ownership**, not technology, and puts his faith in the **union** and public rules.
He refuses **AI tools** and retraining in the fast scenarios, though ten years makes him consider vet tech work.
His mood runs from **anxious** to alarmed, easing only when the kids would be grown.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves a family with **no savings** exposed.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage guarantee** paid for by robot owners, and the **union** at the table before the fund decides.
